1. Patrick Flynn's birthplace is disputed between Ireland (1850 and 1860 censuses) and Pennsylvania (1908 death certificate). Identifying the correct birthplace matters because establishing his origins is necessary background for any search for his parents in Irish records — a wrong birthplace country misdirects the entire inquiry.

2. The 1850 census (a_002) records Patrick, then approximately 5 years old, as born in Ireland. The household informant — almost certainly Thomas Flynn, the head of household — supplied this information to the enumerator five years after the birth. The 1860 census (a_009) again records Patrick, now approximately 15, as born in Ireland. The 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate (a_012) states his birthplace as Pennsylvania; the informant was James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law, who signed the certificate. The attending physician signed only for cause and date of death, not personal details.

3. The census records are more reliable for this fact. Thomas Flynn, and possibly Patrick himself by 1860, had direct family knowledge of where Patrick was born. Their information was recorded 5 and 15 years after the birth, respectively, by two different enumerators, with both agreeing on Ireland. James Brown could not have known Patrick's birthplace firsthand — he married into the family only after Patrick was an adult — and reported a birth he never witnessed, 63 years after the event. 4. The death certificate error reflects a well-documented pattern of immigration origin confusion. Patrick Flynn arrived in Pennsylvania from Ireland as a very young child and lived there for approximately 60 years. By 1908, his son-in-law James Brown knew Patrick exclusively as a Pennsylvania man; Patrick's actual birth in Ireland was distant family history that a son-in-law had no particular reason to have been told or to have retained accurately. Reporting under the immediate stress of a death, Brown substituted the deceased's long-familiar American home for his actual foreign birthplace — a classic example of a secondary informant's local knowledge of the family overriding a biographical fact he could not have witnessed.

Clear picture established. The two assertions (a_001: name "Anders Pedersen"; a_002: birth ~1868, Ringsaker) both come from one 1875 census record. **The decisive finding:** Norway used a live patronymic system in 1875, 48 years before the 1923 surname-fixing law. "Pedersen" encodes *son of Peder*; "Hansen" encodes *son of Hans.* The subject's documented father is **Hans Olsen (I2)** — which generates the patronymic *Hansen*, not *Pedersen*. In a patronymic system this is not a spelling variant: the two forms name different fathers and therefore different children. The matching given name, birth year, and location are fully explained by the traditional Norwegian convention of naming first sons after paternal grandfathers, which routinely produced two or more boys of the same name and age in the same parish from unrelated families.
